A 53-year-old Malawian man presents to a local hospital with a productive cough and whitish sputum for 3 months. He also reports night sweats and some weight loss, which he is unable to quantify. Two months prior, he was treated with presumptive antimalarials and amoxicillin for 5 days without improvement. He denies TB contacts, is a non-smoker, and has no significant past medical history. He is a subsistence farmer, married with five well children.

On examination, his temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F), blood pressure is 100/80 mmHg, pulse is 88 bpm, and oxygen saturation is 97% on ambient air. He appears mildly anaemic. Oral examination reveals no oral thrush, Kaposi’s sarcoma, or oral hairy leukoplakia. His chest is clear with normal heart sounds. There is no lymphadenopathy, and his liver and spleen are not enlarged.

Laboratory results show: WBC 3.2 x10°/L (reference 4-10), Haemoglobin 9.8 g/dL (reference 13-15), MCV 90 fL (reference 80-98), Platelets 305 x10°/L (reference 150-350), CD4 count 54 cells/μL (reference 500-1200), Sputum for AFB 2 x negative (reference Negative), Malaria RDT Negative (reference Negative), Thick smear for Plasmodium spp. Negative (reference Negative).

His chest radiograph on admission shows a prominent hilar region bilaterally but is otherwise normal (Fig. 33.1).

What is your suspected diagnosis?

A 35-year-old woman from Malawi presents to the outpatient department of a local tertiary hospital, referred for exenteration of the left eye due to an ocular tumour. She first noticed a whitish lesion on the conjunctiva of her left eye 8 months prior, which grew bigger and turned reddish despite treatment with unspecified eye drops and herbal remedies. She eventually lost vision in the affected eye, and pain increased. The patient is known to be HIV-positive and has been on antiretroviral treatment for the past 3 years, but her CD4 count is unknown. Clinical examination reveals localized swelling of the left eyeball and orbit, incomplete lid closure (Fig. 43.1), and no light perception in the left eye. Visual acuity on the right side is 6/6. Her left preauricular lymph nodes are swollen. She is afebrile, and the rest of her physical examination is unremarkable. What is the suspected diagnosis?

A 40-year-old farmer from the Peruvian Amazon is referred to a hospital in Lima with a 4-month history of chronic productive cough and chest pain. He reports dyspnoea on exertion and weight loss of about 20 kg. He denies diarrhoea, fever or night sweats. Three and a half months earlier, he was hospitalized for similar complaints and received first-line TB therapy (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol) based on a clinical presentation and abnormal chest radiographic findings, though the report is unavailable. Despite adherence to treatment, he showed no clinical improvement and reported streaking of blood in the sputum. He was then referred to Lima with a suspected diagnosis of multi-drug resistant TB (MDR TB). The patient had been found to be HTLV-1-positive 10 years previously. A recent HIV ELISA test was negative.

On examination, the patient appears fatigued and cachectic. His temperature is 37.2 °C, blood pressure 120/75 mmHg, pulse 70 bpm regular, and respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute. Few cervical and retroauricular lymph nodes are palpable, small, mobile, soft and non-tender. Lungs reveal crackles and rhonchi bilaterally. No hepatosplenomegaly is noted.

Laboratory results show platelets of 1093 x 10^9/L (reference range: 150–450); the rest of the full blood count is within normal limits. The chest X-ray shows bilateral confluent reticulonodular infiltrates and multiple cavities in the right lung (Fig. 55.1).

What are your differential diagnoses?

A 35-year-old Peruvian man is referred to a hospital in Lima after experiencing fever and retro-orbital headache for eight days. Two days into the illness, he was admitted to a local hospital in the jungle due to jaundice, coffee-ground vomiting, gross haematuria, and increasing mental obtundation. During transfer to the referral hospital in Lima, the patient had a generalized seizure. His past medical history includes hepatitis of unknown aetiology 20 years prior. He has been working as a logging supervisor in a remote jungle area near Pucallpa on the shores of the Ucayali River for the past 5 years. He has not taken malaria prophylaxis and has not received any vaccinations since early childhood.

On examination, his temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F), blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, heart rate is 110 beats per minute, and respiratory rate is 24 breaths per minute. He is agitated, unresponsive to verbal commands, and intermittently stuporous, with marked flapping of hands. He is jaundiced, with spontaneous bleeding of his oral mucosa and at venipuncture/IV sites. Multiple large ecchymoses are present on his face, trunk, and limbs (Fig. 93.1). Auscultation reveals crepitant rales in both lung bases. The liver is felt 3 cm below the right costal margin; the spleen is not palpable, and there is no lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory results on admission are as follows: haematocrit 30% (41-53), white cell count 8700/μL (4500-11000) with 4% bands, 62% neutrophils, 0% eosinophils, 0% basophils, 6% monocytes, and 28% lymphocytes; platelets 110000/μL (150000-450000); AST 2890 U/L (0-35), ALT 2676 U/L (0-35); AP 496 U/L (38-126), total bilirubin 11.6 mg/dL (0.3-1.2), direct bilirubin 9.2 mg/dL (0-0.4); urea 89 mg/dL (17-49), creatinine 1.2 mg/dL (0.6-1.2); glucose 80 mg/dL (70-110), serum protein 4.2 g/L (5.5-8.0), albumin 2.8 g/L (3.5-5.5); prothrombin time 17 s (11.1-13.1), INR 2.6 (0.9-1.3), aPTT 80 s (22.1-35.1); fibrinogen 250 mg/dL (150-400); CK 6200 U/L (52-336); urine proteins 3+, RBC 50-60/f, WBC 4-6/f. Malaria thick film is three times negative. Blood cultures are negative. Brucella serology is negative. Hepatitis B IgM anti-Hbc are negative.

What is your differential diagnosis?

A 35-year-old Malawian woman presents to a local hospital because of fever and weakness. The fever started 3 days earlier, but the weakness has progressed over the past several months. There is no cough and no night sweats, but she reports some weight loss. There is no diarrhoea, no dysuria and no history of abnormal bleeds. Two months earlier she presented to a local health centre because of her weakness and was found to be clinically pale and was prescribed iron tablets, which she took, but the weakness progressed. She is divorced, with three children (17, 15 and 12 years old), who are all well. She works as a small-scale farmer and sells vegetables on the local market. The family can afford three meals a day and occasionally meat or fish.

On examination, she is wasted, with a BMI of 17 kg/m². Her blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg, pulse 110 bpm, temperature 37.8°C, respiratory rate 25 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97% on ambient air, and Glasgow Coma Scale 15/15. Her conjunctivae are very pale, but there is no jaundice. The chest is clear. The abdomen is soft, with slight diffuse tenderness, but no guarding. The spleen is palpable 3 cm below the left costal margin. The rectal examination is normal.

Investigations reveal a negative malaria rapid diagnostic test and a positive HIV serology. Her full blood count shows a WBC count of 3.0 x10^9/L, hemoglobin of 4.8 mg/dL, MCV of 90 fL, and platelet count of 112 x10^9/L (Table 29.1).

What is the suspected diagnosis?

A previously healthy 20-year-old man from southern India is admitted to a local hospital with fever and quadriparesis. He has had fever for 4 days, followed by tingling and weakness initially in his left leg, subsequently involving all four limbs over the next 2 days. He gives a history of a stray dog bite (WHO category III) on his left lower limb 1 month before onset of symptoms, for which he received five doses of anti-rabies vaccine (purified chick embryo cell vaccine), but no rabies immunoglobulin (RIG). On admission, he is conscious and his mental functions are normal (GCS 15/15). His blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, pulse 90 beats per minute, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and temperature 38.5 °C (101.3 °F). Neurological examination reveals a flaccid, areflexic quadriparesis. His blood investigations including serum electrolytes, renal and liver function test are normal. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) shows 52 mg/dL protein (reference: 15-50 mg/dL), 60 mg/dL glucose (reference: 50-75 mg, provided a normal serum glucose) and 340 cells/mm³ (60% polymorphs and 40% lymphocytes; normal ≤5 cells/mm³). Consider Table 91.1 (Fig 1) and Table 91.2 (Fig 2). What is the final diagnosis?

A 25-year-old Malawian primary school teacher presents with abrupt onset of fever and confusion. She was well at 8 a.m., confused by 10 a.m., and drowsy with a high fever and convulsions on admission at 11 a.m. She is HIV-positive and has been on first-line ART (tenofovir, lamivudine, efavirenz) for 6 months with good adherence. Her CD4 count on starting ART was 320 cells/µL. She completed treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis 2 months ago. On examination, she is restless and agitated with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 10/15. Pupils are equal and reactive with photophobia; the neck is stiff and there is no rash. Plantar responses are down-going, Kernig’s sign is positive. Temperature is 40°C (104°F), pulse is 125 bpm, blood pressure is 125/68 mmHg, and oxygen saturation is 93% on room air. She suffers a renewed seizure during the physical examination. Blood results show WBC 10.5 x10°/L (reference 4-10), neutrophil count 8.9 x10°/L (reference 2.5-6), hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL (reference 12-14), MCV 85 fL (reference 78-90), platelets 255 x10⁹/L (reference 150-400), creatinine 106 µmol/L (reference 35-106), and random blood glucose 5.6 mmol/L (reference 3.9-7.8). A spinal tap was performed, revealing hazy CSF. CSF results show leukocytes 35 cells/µL (60% neutrophils) (reference 0-5/µL), protein 2.6 g/L (reference 0.15-0.42), and glucose 1.2 mmol/L (reference 2.5-5). Rapid antigen test for Plasmodium falciparum is negative. What are your treatment priorities for this woman?

A 51-year-old female Swiss traveller presented to the outpatient department 6 days after returning from a 2-week holiday to Guatemala and El Salvador. Four days after her return, the patient noticed a generalized slightly pruritic maculopapular rash on the face, trunk, and extremities. There was no fever and no other accompanying symptoms. On the next day the rash worsened and a non-purulent bilateral conjunctivitis developed. The patient did not report any chronic underlying disease nor the intake of any medication. Upon inspection there was conjunctivitis and a generalised maculopapular rash, also involving the face. Additionally, the patient showed tender oedema of the hands, elbows, knees and feet (Fig. 77.1). There was also generalized lymphadenopathy (cervical, axillary, and inguinal). The full blood count was normal. CRP was $8 \mathrm { m g / L } ( < 5 )$ and creatinine was very mildly elevated $( 8 7 \mu \mathrm { m o l } / \mathrm { L }$ , range $3 5 { - } 8 0$ $\mu \mathrm { m o l } / \mathrm { L } )$ . Liver function tests were normal. What are your differential diagnoses?

A 24-year-old man of Turkish origin presents with right upper quadrant pain, nausea and vomiting. He has a history of right upper quadrant pain three years prior, when an ultrasound and CT scan revealed two calcified cystic lesions in the liver (Fig. 50.1 and Fig. 50.2). Serology was positive for Echinococcus granulosus, and a diagnosis of cystic echinococcosis (CE) was made. Anthelmintic treatment was not considered due to cyst wall calcification. The cysts were monitored by ultrasound. Currently, he presents with right upper quadrant and epigastric tenderness, but no guarding. His vital signs are: blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, pulse 64 bpm, temperature 36°C. Laboratory findings are as follows: AST 145 U/L, ALT 454 U/L, GGT 394 U/L, ALP 402 U/L, total bilirubin 120 μmol/L, ESR 17/40 mm/h, and CRP 49 mg/L (Table 50.1). What is the suspected diagnosis and how would you approach this patient?

A 22-year-old male farmer from rural northern Ethiopia presents to a hospital with difficulty walking. His problem started 10 years ago, when he woke from sleep one morning and noticed weakness in both legs. The weakness rapidly progressed over 4 to 5 days, leading to him needing a cane for mobility. He had no back pain, sensory complaints, sphincter disturbance or upper limb symptoms. The onset of his illness coincided with a period of drought and famine, when his diet almost exclusively consisted of grass peas (local name), which is Lathyrus sativus (Fig. 69.1). Despite the monotonous diet, he had been engaged in hard physical labour. Several similar cases of weakness among young male farmers occurred in his village. He moved to the capital city at the age of 20 seeking an alternative job, along with another young male farmer from his village who had suffered a similar fate.

On examination, he is an alert young man with a normal mental state. His gait is spastic (‘scissor gait’), with foot-dragging and toe-scraping (Fig. 69.2). There is mild bilateral lower limb spastic weakness of pyramidal pattern, with pathological brisk deep tendon reflexes and sustained foot clonus. Extensor plantar response is elicited on the right, while equivocal on the left. Cranial nerves and upper limbs are normal. There is no sensory or bladder dysfunction.

Full blood count, liver and renal function tests, cerebrospinal fluid, nerve conduction studies and electromyography are normal. His HIV-1 serology is non-reactive. HTLV-1 and -2 serology and MRI are not available.

What clinical syndrome can you apply for a diagnostic approach and how do you narrow down your differential diagnoses?

A 45-year-old Sri Lankan man presents to a local hospital with fever, chills, headache, body aches and severe right hypochondrial pain for the past week. He has also developed a dry cough during the past few days. He has vomited twice during his illness and has lost his appetite. His abdominal pain is constant and dull, radiating to the right shoulder and worsened by coughing and resting on the right side. He admits to consuming locally brewed alcohol (todd) daily for the past 10 to 15 years. On examination, he appears generally ill, mildly dehydrated, and in pain. His temperature is 38.3°C (100.8°F), blood pressure 100/80 mmHg, pulse 102 bpm, and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. There is no jaundice, pallor, or lymphadenopathy. Abdominal examination reveals a tender hepatomegaly, with tenderness most prominent over the 6th to 9th intercostal spaces in the right midaxillary line. The spleen is not enlarged. Auscultation reveals few inspiratory crackles over the right lung base. Cardiovascular and nervous systems are normal. Laboratory results are shown in Table 46.1. What is the likely diagnosis?

A 23-year-old HIV-positive Zambian woman is referred to a local teaching hospital in Lusaka after suffering her first ever seizure. The seizure occurred out of sleep, with the patient found unresponsive and shaking all four limbs for 5 to 10 minutes. She was diagnosed with HIV infection 1 month earlier and is not yet on antiretroviral therapy (ART) but has been taking co-trimoxazole prophylaxis for 7 days. She was successfully treated for pulmonary tuberculosis 4 years ago. On examination, she looks well, with a GCS score of 15/15, normal vital signs, and no meningism. The chest is clear, and the neurological examination is unremarkable. Laboratory results show a WBC count of 5.8 x 10°/L, hemoglobin of 11.0 g/dL, platelets of 215 x 10°/L, CD4 count of 153 cells/μL, serum sodium of 135 mmol/L, and serum glucose of 4.5 mmol/L (Table 75.1). A lumbar puncture was performed with a normal opening pressure. The CSF is clear, with 5 leukocytes/μL, protein of 0.78 g/L, glucose of 2.9 mmol/L, negative cryptococcal antigen, negative India Ink stain, negative Gram stain, and negative Ziehl-Neelsen stain (Table 75.2). Electroencephalography (EEG) demonstrates focal slowing in the right hemisphere (Fig. 75.1). A CT scan of her brain shows frontal and parietal hypodense lesions in the white matter of the right hemisphere (Fig. 75.2). No contrast enhancement is present.

What is your general approach to a patient presenting with new-onset seizures in sub-Saharan Africa?

A 28-year-old West African man presents to a clinic in Ghana complaining of a painful ulcer on his left ankle (Fig. 62.1). The ulcer has been present for the past 4 months and is not healing. He has a history of a previous ulcer on his right ankle some years ago which took about a year to heal. He also complains of pain in his right thigh and in both knees. On examination, the patient is short for an adult, pale and has a tinge of jaundice. The ulcer is on his left ankle, next to the medial malleolus; the skin surrounding it is hyperpigmented. There is tenderness in both knee joints and in his right thigh. Vital signs: Temperature 36.6°C, pulse 88 bpm, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg. Laboratory results are shown in Table 62.1, and the patient’s blood film is shown in Fig. 62.2. What is your differential diagnosis?

A 40-year-old Thai woman presents to an outpatient clinic in Germany with a history of severe headache for the past 8 days. The headache was of gradual onset and did not respond to any painkillers. There is no fever and no chills. She denies any visual problems, any weakness of her limbs or memory problems. Ten days earlier she had returned from a 4-week journey to north-east Thailand, where she visited friends and relatives. During her visit she ate traditional regional dishes, including freshwater fish, seafood, snails and frogs. She reports that her brother-in-law, with whom she had shared several traditional meals, has also fallen ill with a severe headache. She presented to a municipal hospital 3 days earlier. A CT scan of her brain was performed and reported to be normal. Her blood count was also normal. Her past medical history is unremarkable. On examination, she is afebrile, her neck is supple and Lasè-gue’s sign (straight leg raise) is negative. Pupils are equal, round and react to light and accommodation, and there are no cranial nerve palsies. The remainder of the neurological examination, including the assessment of higher cortical functions such as language, memory and praxia, is unremarkable. There is no rash, no oral thrush and there are no subcutaneous swellings. Cardiopulmonary examination is normal. Liver and spleen are not enlarged, and there is no lymphadenopathy. Her laboratory results at presentation in the clinic are shown in Table 64.1 (WBC 12.3 x 10°/L, Eosinophils 2.34 x 10⁹/L, Haemoglobin 11.7 mg/dL, MCV 70 fL, Platelets 330 x 10⁹/L, ESR 20 mm/h, IgE 944 U/mL, Creatinine 62 umol/L, ALT 28 U/L, C-reactive protein <5 mg/L). What is your presumptive diagnosis?

A 24-year-old Malawian businessman presents with dark spots on his arm and leg for the last month, which are progressing and accompanied by facial swelling. He also reports a 3-month history of cough and worsening shortness of breath, without constitutional symptoms like weight loss, fevers, or night sweats. His cough is productive of white sputum, and he has no history of previous tuberculosis. He recently tested positive for HIV and has not yet started antiretroviral medication. On examination, he appears comfortable at rest with moderate facial oedema (Fig. 59.1). His temperature is 36°C (96.8°F), respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and pulse 102 bpm. Widespread dark-purplish plaques are noted on the skin (Fig. 59.1) and palate. Respiratory examination reveals decreased air entry and dullness at the right lung base. He has swelling of his right leg from the foot to the knee, with prominent dark plaques which are coalescing (Fig. 59.2). His CD4 count is 134 cells/µL, HB 10.2 g/dL and MCV 88.4 fL. His chest radiograph shows bilateral patchy opacifications in the lower and mid zones of the lungs (Fig. 59.3). Sputum and GeneXpert tests were negative for tuberculosis. What are your most important differential diagnoses?

A 4-year-old boy from rural Mozambique presents with a 5-day history of suspected nephrotic syndrome, unresponsive to furosemide and prednisolone. He was previously treated for pneumonia 3 weeks prior. Clinical examination reveals a miserable, apathetic child with a puffy face and pitting edema on the lower legs. His hair is brittle, sparse, and fair, and his skin is dry, hyperpigmented, and peeling off like ‘flaky paint’ (Fig. 72.1). Ulcerative skin lesions are present, particularly in the groins (Fig. 72.2). Laboratory results show an albumin level of 2.2 g/dL (reference range 3.0-5.2 g/dL) and a hemoglobin level of 7 g/dL (reference range 12-14 g/dL). What is the likely diagnosis and how can it be distinguished from nephrotic syndrome?

A 44-year-old male rice farmer presents to a provincial hospital in Southern Laos in the rainy season with a 1-month history of fever, headache, generalized myalgia and arthralgia and a painful swelling over the left scapula. The swelling has gradually increased in size, without any history of preceding trauma. He has not noticed any lesions elsewhere. He was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes 4 years previously but was not compliant with oral antidiabetic drugs or follow-up. The lesion on his back was incised and drained at a local health centre the previous week, since when he has been taking cloxacillin 1 g four times daily. However, there has been no improvement and during the 2 days prior to admission he has deteriorated, with high fever, chills and severe malaise.

On examination, the patient appears septic, with a fever of 40 °C (104 °F), a heart rate of 136 bpm, blood pressure of 140/80 mmHg and a respiratory rate of 30 breath cycles per minute. He is pale and jaundiced. In the left scapular region, there is an erythematous swelling of 2.5 x 4 cm with pus discharging from a central wound (Fig. 32.1). There is no regional lymphadenopathy. On chest auscultation there are bilateral crepitations and reduced breath sounds at both lung bases. Heart sounds are normal. The abdomen is soft, without any palpable organomegaly.

Laboratory results are as follows: WBC 16.2 x10º/L, Polymorphs 92.1%, Haemoglobin 12.5 g/dL, Platelets 112 x10/L, Glucose 20.6 mmol/L, Serum creatinine 56 μmol/L, Urea 6.8 mmol/L, AST 131 U/L, ALT 83 U/L, Serum total bilirubin 111.2 umol/L, Serum direct bilirubin 56.4 μmol/L (Table 32.1).

What are your differential diagnoses?

A 34-year-old Malawian woman presents to a neurology outpatient clinic with slowly progressive weakness of the left arm and leg, starting approximately 3 months prior with a limp in her left leg. The weakness progressed to affect her left arm. She denies head trauma, headache, fever, nausea, visual impairment, or weight loss. She was diagnosed with smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis 5 months earlier and found to be HIV-reactive with a baseline CD4 count of 54/µL. She was started on antituberculous therapy, vitamin B6, antiretroviral therapy, and co-trimoxazole prophylaxis, all of which she is currently taking.

On examination, she is afebrile with normal vital signs and slightly pale conjunctivae. Fundoscopy is normal. Neurological examination reveals a spastic hemiparesis on the left with hyperreflexia. Power in the left leg is 2/5, and in the left arm 3/5, with pronator drift on the left (Fig. 51.1). Sensation of pain is reduced in her left leg and hand. Cranial nerves are normal.

Laboratory results show: WBC 3.8 x 10^9/L (4–10), hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL (12–14), platelets 140 x 10^9/L (150–350).

What is your differential diagnosis?

A 29-year-old woman is brought to a hospital in Malawi by her relatives. She has been confused, restless and irritable for the past month. She also has watery diarrhoea, which started 1 week ago. She does not have a fever. It is January, which is the rainy season in Malawi. Her past medical history has been uneventful. There have been no psychiatric disorders in the past. Her HIV status is unknown. She is not taking any medication. There are no known intoxications, no use of alcohol or recreational drugs. The patient is married with four children and is a housewife. Her husband works as a farmhand on a local chicken farm. They live in a grass-thatched mud-hut and collect their water from a borehole. There is no electricity at home. They eat two meals a day, mainly maize porridge with a few vegetables. Only rarely can the family afford fish or meat.

On examination, the patient is slim but not wasted. Glasgow Coma Scale 14/15 (confusion), the remaining vital signs are normal and she is afebrile. There is no neck stiffness. The conjunctivae are pale. There is a noticeable skin rash around the patient’s neck (Fig. 37.1), on her forearms, hands and feet (Fig. 37.2), where the skin appears hyperpigmented and dry. The skin changes are clearly demarcated. The rest of the physical examination is unremarkable. Her relatives report that the rash had been present for the past 2 months.

What is the suspected diagnosis and what are your differential diagnoses?

A 37-year-old woman from the Lower Shire Valley in southern Malawi is referred to the district hospital after vomiting blood three times over the past 24 hours. The blood is bright red, and she denies epigastric pain, fever, or abnormal bleeding. Her stool is normal in color. She has no history of NSAID or alcohol use. Her past medical history is unremarkable, and she lives and works on a sugar plantation. She is married with three healthy children. An HIV test 3 months prior was negative. On examination, she is slim but not wasted, with slightly pale conjunctivae. Her blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg, pulse 110 bpm, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and she is afebrile. Abdominal examination reveals no distension or tenderness, but the spleen is palpable 10 cm below the left costal margin. The liver is slightly enlarged, with no stigmata of chronic liver disease or shifting dullness. Lymph nodes are not enlarged. Laboratory results show a WBC count of 2.8 x 10^9/L, hemoglobin of 8.3 g/dL, MCV of 88 fL, and platelet count of 130 x 10^9/L (Table 57.1). (Fig. 57.1) What is the most likely cause of her haematemesis?

A 14-year-old boy presents to his local hospital in rural Tanzania with a history of difficulty in walking. He had been well until just over 2 years earlier when his illness suddenly started. He describes that he was walking home from school when he first noticed that his legs began to feel heavy and started to tremble, which caused him difficulty in walking, with a tendency to fall over. He now stands on his toes and drags his legs around with the aid of a stick (Fig. 24.1). He denies any history of fever, pain, sensory, bladder or bowel symptoms or disease progression. He lives in a village in northern Tanzania in a rural area with limited agricultural suitability, where the main staple food crop is cassava. His diet for the 2 months before the illness was almost exclusively cassava. He has three other siblings, one of whom is similarly affected, whereas their parents remained fine. He mentions that identical cases had occurred in his own and neighbouring villages at around the same time.

Clinically, he is well nourished with normal vital signs. General examination is unremarkable. On neurological examination, he is fully orientated and higher mental function appears normal. Cranial nerves are normal but bilateral optic pallor was noted on fundoscopy. Limbs reveal signs of spastic paraparesis with flexion contractures at both ankles and knees. Power in the legs is graded 3 to 4 out of 5, with the knee extensors and foot dorsiflexors involved to the greatest extent (Fig. 24.1). There is bilateral hypertonia, hyperreflexia and sustained ankle clonus with extensor plantar responses. The arms are normal apart from generalized hyperreflexia. There is no impairment or loss of sensation. A lumbar lordosis with thoracic kyphoscoliosis is noticeable only on standing.

Full blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, blood glucose and creatinine are normal. Urine analysis is normal. Microscopy of urine and stool specimens does not show any ova of Schistosoma species. HIV serology and VDRL are negative. Lumbar puncture is normal. Radiographs of the chest and thoracolumbar spine are normal.

What is the clinical diagnosis and the likely cause in this patient?

A 40-year-old man from Togo presents to a local clinic with a 4-year history of changes in both eyes, without visual disturbances, but concerned about blindness prevalent in his village. He also reports painless bumps under his skin developing over two decades, and intense itching. He has always lived in a village near a fast-flowing river, where biting flies are common. Clinical examination reveals opacities in the cornea of both eyes (Fig. 19.1), atrophic skin with scratch marks, and palpable subcutaneous nodules (1-3 cm) over bony prominences like the ribs (Fig. 19.2), iliac crest, femoral trochanters, and head. The nodules are firm and non-tender.

What is your most important differential diagnosis?

A 30-year-old woman presents to the outpatient clinic of a hospital in Spain. She was born in Santa Cruz (Bolivia) and arrived in Europe 4 months prior. She has been living in an urban environment for the past 20 years but grew up in a rural area during her childhood. She reports a 2-year history of progressive dyspnoea at moderate exertion (New York Heart Association grade II) along with self-limiting palpitations. She has no other relevant medical history and does not take any medication. She expresses the wish to become pregnant.

On examination, the blood pressure is 110/65 mmHg. The pulse is regular at 40 bpm. SpO2 is 99% on ambient air. On auscultation, cardiac sounds are clear and there are no murmurs. The chest is clear. There is no peripheral oedema and the jugular venous pressure is not raised.

Full blood count and basic blood chemistry tests are normal. Her ECG is shown in Fig. 89.1. Her chest radiograph is shown in Fig. 89.1B.

In a recent migrant from Bolivia, which different pathologies should be screened for?

A 74-year-old Japanese man is brought to a hospital with a 5-day history of fever, joint pain, headache, and nausea. He has a history of cerebral infarction without neurological sequelae, hypertension, and ulcerative colitis. He is currently taking antiplatelet medication, antihypertensive medication, and adalimumab (TNF-alpha blocker) via subcutaneous injection every 2 weeks. He lives in a suburb of a city in Kyushu district, southwestern Japan, and has opportunities to encounter wild animals such as boars and deer. He is retired and does grape farming occasionally. He denies recent overseas travel.

On examination, the patient appears unwell and drowsy. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse rate is 101 bpm, blood pressure is 120/70 mmHg, SpO2 is 96% with 7L of oxygen, and respiratory rate is 32 breaths per minute. Chest examination is normal. His Glasgow Coma Scale is 13/15 (E3V4M6). Livedo reticularis is present bilaterally on his lower extremities, but no rash is observed. His left inguinal lymph node is enlarged.

Laboratory results on admission are as follows (Table 88.1): WBC 5.3 × 10°/L, Haemoglobin 17.7 g/dL, Platelets 90 × 10°/L, AST 413 U/L, ALT 95 U/L, LDH 1025 U/L, CK 7442 U/L, CK-MB 41 U/L, and CRP 0.1 mg/dL.

What are your differential diagnosis and diagnostic approach?

A 38-year-old European expatriate presents at the medical outpatient clinic in a tertiary hospital in Malawi with progressive constipation and difficulty passing urine for the past 3 weeks. He noticed that he had to use increasing abdominal pressure to pass urine and eventually became only able to pass small amounts at a time. This is associated with increasing lower abdominal discomfort, abnormal sensations in the groins and around the genitals and some erectile dysfunction. He has no weakness and there is no dysaesthesia and no loss of sensation in his legs. However, he mentions that walking did not feel normal, although he cannot fully explain what the abnormality is. He has no backache. Over the past 2 months he has experienced unintentional weight loss of $8 \mathrm { k g }$ and fatigue without fever or night sweats. He has sexual contact with his wife only, to whom he has been married for several years. One week prior to presentation he had noticed reddish discoloration of his urine. He had no painful micturition or fever at that time. He visited a local clinic and was prescribed four different types of medication, which he completed. There is no history of trauma and the rest of his previous medical history is unremarkable.

On physical examination, he looks healthy and has normal vital signs. There are no abnormalities on general examination, except for a palpable bladder. The rectal examination reveals a low anal sphincter tone and the genital examination is normal. He has lively, symmetrical tendon reflexes in the legs without clonus or pathological plantar reflexes, and no abnormalities in the rest of the neurological examination.

A full blood count showed a normal absolute WBC of $9 \times 10^9/L$ with a relative eosinophilia of $21.8\%$ (reference range: $1-6\%$) and an absolute eosinophil count of $1.15 \times 10^9/L$ (reference: $<0.45 \times 10^9/L$). ALT was slightly elevated. Creatinine and CRP were normal. An HIV test and the VDRL were negative. An MRI scan of the spinal cord was performed (Fig. 63.1). An enhancing $1 \mathrm { cm}$ large lesion was seen at the anterior aspect of the conus, with associated high T2 signal representing oedema extending from the lower end of the conus to the level of T9. In addition, there was nodular thickening of the urine bladder wall at the base and the posterior aspect.

What are possible diagnoses and which investigations would you order?

A 31-year-old HIV-positive man presents to the Emergency Department with a 6-week history of increasing shortness of breath on exertion, dry cough, and drenching night sweats. He also reports fatigue and a weight loss of 10 kg over the past 5 months. He travels extensively for business, having recently visited Europe, China, Korea, Japan, Singapore, and the United States. He denies recreational drug use and has never smoked. He was diagnosed with HIV 6 years ago, with a CD4 count of 280/µL one month prior to presentation. He is not currently on antiretroviral therapy (ART) or co-trimoxazole prophylaxis. On examination, he is alert but short of breath at rest, with a temperature of 39.2°C (102.6°F), blood pressure of 120/70 mmHg, pulse of 100 bpm, respiratory rate of 26 breaths per minute, SpO2 of 87% on air, and 97% on 15 L O2. Chest auscultation is clear. His arterial blood gases on air are pH 7.44, PaO2 7.6 kPa, PaCO2 3 kPa, HCO3 19 mmol/L, base excess -3.8 mmol/L, and lactate 1.6 mmol/L (Table 23.1). His FBC is normal, CRP is 6.7 mg/dL (<5), and creatinine, urea, bilirubin, ALT, AP, and albumin are normal. CD4 count is 150/µL, and HIV viral load is 1,500,000 copies/mL. His chest radiograph (Fig. 23.1) shows bilateral perihilar infiltrates.

What further investigations would you perform in order to confirm the diagnosis?

A 25-year-old woman from Bani Suwaif in Upper Egypt presents with severe diarrhoea for 2 months accompanied by weight loss of about 15 kg and amenorrhoea. The symptoms started with stomach rumbles and colicky abdominal pain, later progressing to anorexia and vomiting. The diarrhoea is voluminous, not related to meals, and occurs both during the day and at night (five to ten times in 24 hours). She received various antibiotics, including metronidazole, and antidiarrhoeal drugs without improvement. During the last month, she developed lower limb swelling and severe prostration.

Clinical examination reveals a generally unwell patient who is pale with angular stomatitis. She is afebrile, with a heart rate of 100 bpm, blood pressure of 100/60 mmHg, a scaphoid abdomen with borborygmi, pitting oedema of the lower limbs, and decreased skin turgor.

Laboratory results are summarized in Table 58.1 (see image). D-xylose test shows evidence of malabsorption. On stool microscopy, numerous helminth ova are detected (Fig. 58.1) ![](images/ed24f94a689d80e55c3502e2436649aa7128a306dfaf8cd88f17bc2f0a0f2d4f.jpg).

Which helminth is causing the patient’s clinical problems and why is it able to cause such severe infections?

A 58-year-old Sri Lankan woman presents with a 10-day history of high-grade fever, chills, body aches, non-productive cough, and progressive shortness of breath. Two days prior, she developed tinnitus and hearing loss, followed by increasing confusion one day before admission. On examination, she is confused (GCS 13/15), with severely impaired hearing (WHO grade 3). Her temperature is 39.3°C (102.7°F), heart rate is 120 bpm, and blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg. There are enlarged axillary lymph nodes on the right side. Auscultation reveals scattered crackles over both lung bases. Her liver is enlarged to 5 cm below the right costal margin, and the spleen is just palpable. Laboratory results show a WBC count of 8.5 (4-10), hemoglobin of 12.4 (12-16), platelets of 98 (150-350), AST of 74 (13-33), ALT of 68 (3-25), ALP of 126 (40-130), total bilirubin of 25.7, blood urea nitrogen of 6.4 (2.5-6.4), creatinine of 123.8 (71-106), and C-reactive protein of 48 (<6). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis reveals 35 leukocytes (80% lymphocytes) (0-5/L), protein of 0.64 (0.15-0.45), and glucose of 3.25 mmol/L (paired random blood glucose 7.17 mmol/L). Blood cultures are negative, Leptospira serologies are negative, and a malaria smear is negative. Chest radiography shows no pathological changes, and ECG reveals sinus tachycardia. EEG shows widespread slowing, and CT scan of the brain is normal. (Fig 70.1, Fig 70.2)

What clinical sign will you be specifically looking for?

A 24-year-old woman presents to a small hospital in rural Uganda because of a 5-day history of a febrile illness. Apart from fever, the illness started with a sore throat and aching all over. She also developed some abdominal pain and diarrhoea. The patient has become increasingly unwell over the course of the past days. She is very weak and needs help to stand. Her husband died of a severe febrile illness 6 days before she became ill. He had worked in a local gold mine and had previously been in good health. He had fallen ill about a week before his death. His wife had looked after him during his final illness and he had died at home.

On examination, the patient looks very unwell. Her blood pressure is 85/65 mmHg, pulse rate 105 bpm, temperature 38°C (100.4°F). She has bilateral conjunctivitis. There is no rash and no lymphadenopathy. The heart sounds are normal and her chest is clear. Her abdominal examination is normal.

What are your differential diagnoses?

An 18-year-old man from India has noticed a pale patch on his right arm and forearm for 3 months. It is not itchy or painful, but he reports reduced sensation in the affected area. He also complains of mild numbness of the little finger of the right hand but no weakness (he is right-handed). There is no family history of skin problems. On examination, there is a 20 cm by 10 cm hypopigmented macule on the outer aspect of the right arm extending on to the forearm (Fig. 83.1). The affected skin is dry. The sensation within the hypopigmented area is reduced compared with the normally pigmented skin. The rest of the skin examination is normal. Both ulnar nerves are palpable, however the right ulnar nerve is thickened. There is reduced sensation on the tip and ulnar border of the right little finger. There are no other neurological abnormalities. What common skin conditions cause hypopigmentation?

A 26-year-old Malawian woman is brought to the emergency department by relatives. She has been unwell for at least 1 week, complaining of a headache of insidious onset and confusion for 2 days. One day prior to presentation, relatives noticed an eyelid drooping on the left side. Her past medical history is unremarkable. She lives in an urban high-density area and works as a businesswoman. She has three healthy children, but four died as toddlers. Her husband died a year ago of ‘high fever.’ On examination, she appears seriously unwell with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 14/15, temperature of 38.4°C (101.1°F), blood pressure of 115/75 mmHg, heart rate of 86 bpm, and respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute. There is no neck stiffness, and the chest is clear (Fig. 3.1). Blood results are as follows: WBC 3.2 x10^9/L, Hb 10.2 g/dL, Platelets 155 x10^9/L, Serum glucose 4.0 mmol/L, Thick film for malaria and trypanosomes are negative (Table 3.1). A lumbar puncture was performed with an opening pressure of 32 cmH2O. CSF results show a white cell count of 54/μL, CSF protein of 3.0 g/L, and CSF glucose of 1.3 mmol/L (Table 3.2). What is the clinical syndrome and what is the differential diagnosis?

A 7-year-old girl from South Sudan presents with a 4-week history of undulating fever, primarily occurring in the afternoon with chills and occasional convulsions. Initially, she was well between febrile episodes, but has progressively developed anorexia, dry cough, chest pain, joint and back pain. She has no prior hospitalizations but recently received unspecified tablets with no improvement. On examination, she is alert, pale, and severely malnourished (Z-score < 3). Her vital signs are: temperature 39.6°C (103.3°F), pulse 96 bpm, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg. Chest sounds are clear, heart sounds are normal, and the abdomen is soft with splenomegaly of 4 cm below the left costal margin. Multiple enlarged lymph nodes (approximately 1 cm in diameter) are present in the cervical, axillary, inguinal, and epitrochlear regions. There are no skin lesions or peripheral edema. Laboratory results show: WBC 1.35 x10^9/L (reference 4-10), Hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL (reference 12-16), and Platelets 98 x10^9/L (reference 150-300) (Table 44.1). Plasmodium falciparum RDT and blood film are negative. Brucella serology (IgG and IgM) is negative. Visceral leishmaniasis rK39-antibody RDT is negative. 

What are your most important differential diagnoses?

A 20-year-old housewife presents to a hospital in northern Uganda with a 2-day history of fever, severe asthenia, chest and abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and slight non-productive cough. The patient is a Sudanese refugee living in a camp in the region. She denies any contact with sick people. On admission, she is prostrate and semiconscious. Vital signs: temperature 39.6°C (103.3°F), blood pressure 90/60 mmHg, pulse 90 bpm, and respiratory rate 24 cycles per minute. Physical examination revealed abdominal tenderness, especially in the right upper quadrant, hepatosplenomegaly and bleeding from the gums. The lungs were clear. No rash or lymphadenopathy was noted. Intravenous fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics and analgesics were begun. The patient’s condition rapidly worsened, with subconjunctival haemorrhage, copious bleeding from the mouth, nose and rectum (Fig. 1.1) and Fig. 1.2), dyspnoea and hypothermic shock (temperature 36.0°C, blood pressure = unreadable, pulse 150 bpm, respiratory rate 36 cycles per minute). She became comatose and died approximately 24 hours after admission. No clinical laboratory data were available.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 20-year-old woman from the Democratic Republic of the Congo presents with a history of fever, malaise, headache, dry cough, swelling of the neck, and a disseminated skin rash that appeared 2 days after the onset of symptoms. The skin lesions initially appeared on the face and spread centrifugally over her body, including the palms and soles of her feet, as well as the oral mucosa. The lesions have progressed from macules to papules, vesicles, and finally to pustules. The oral mucosal lesions are painful, making drinking and eating difficult. The patient resides in a village and has no relevant past medical history. Her vital signs are: temperature 38°C (100.4°F), pulse 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 105/82 mmHg. Physical examination reveals disseminated uniform umbilicated vesiculopustular skin lesions, ranging from 0.5 to 1 cm in diameter, all over the body with a predilection for the face, hands, and feet (Fig. 94.1). Generalized lymphadenopathy is present, with prominent swelling of the cervical lymph nodes. Lung, heart, abdomen, and CNS examinations are unremarkable. Laboratory results show a WBC count of 4.4 x 10^9/L (73% neutrophils, 21% lymphocytes), hemoglobin of 12.3 g/dL, and ESR of 75 mm/h (Table 94.1).

What are your differential diagnoses?

You review a 6-year-old boy in the paediatric high dependency unit of a Malawian Central Hospital. The boy was admitted the night before because of high fever, dyspnoea and a dry cough which had started 3 days before. On admission, he was started on presumptive antimalarial treatment; the results of the malaria smear are pending. The boy is known to be HIV-positive but is not yet on antiretroviral therapy (ART). Examination reveals a sick child with a temperature of $39.8 ^\circ C$ (103.6 $^\circ F$) and laboured breathing. The Blantyre coma score is 3/5. The boy has coryza and bilateral conjunctivitis. Behind both ears and on the forehead, you notice a fine maculopapular rash that has not been described before. There is bilateral axillary lymphadenopathy. What is your differential diagnosis?

A 34-year-old man from Phuket, Thailand presents to a hospital in Germany with a 2-week history of fever and a 3-month history of weight loss (7 kg). He arrived in Germany 3 days prior to presentation. On examination, the patient is febrile (38.2°C) and appears wasted, with a BMI of 14 kg/m². His conjunctivae are pale. He has a generalized, non-pruritic rash, predominantly on his face and trunk, consisting of small umbilicated papules (Fig. 17.1). There is generalized lymphadenopathy, with visibly swollen lymph nodes in the left supraclavicular region, as well as enlarged inguinal and axillary nodes. The spleen is palpable two fingers below the left costal margin, and the liver span is 15 cm in the midclavicular line. Laboratory results show a WBC count of 2.1 x 10^9/L (reference range 4–10), hemoglobin of 9.8 g/dL (13–16), platelets of 110 x 10^9/L (150–350), and a C-reactive protein of 150 mg/L (<5). What is the single most important test to be done in this patient?

A 55-year-old woman of Turkish provenance presents to a hospital in Germany with intermittent fever up to $39.5^\circ \text{C}$ (103.1$^\circ \text{F}$), night sweats, chest pain, and fatigue. The patient had visited her relatives in Turkey several weeks before. There is a history of rheumatic fever in her childhood and mechanical mitral and aortic valve replacement at the age of 37 and 53 years, respectively (St Jude Medical prostheses). Her blood pressure and heart rate are within normal limits. There are unremarkable prosthetic heart sounds and a systolic grade 1 murmur over the aortic area without radiation. Liver and spleen are not enlarged. No lymph nodes are palpable. No haemorrhages or petechiae are detectable. Laboratory results show slight anaemia ($\text{Hb } 11.5 \text{ g/dL}$ [reference ${ > } 12 \text{ g/dL}$]), normal white blood cell count, lymphocyte–neutrophil ratio, and platelet count. The C-reactive protein is $15 \text{ mg/dL}$ (reference ${ < } 0.5 \text{ mg/dL}$). Serum creatinine and transaminases are not elevated. Blood cultures are negative. Urinary cultures yield Enterobacteriaceae. Chest radiography shows no infiltrates. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrates competent prosthetic valves. The patient is diagnosed with a urinary tract infection and treated with co-trimoxazole. Her fever settles and the patient’s condition improves, but she complains of increasing dyspnoea and eventually slips into congestive heart failure. What are differential diagnoses in this patient after deterioration?

A 33-year-old male refugee from Afghanistan presents to a German clinic with a 6-month history of recurrent fever, night sweats and progressive back pain. After leaving Afghanistan with his wife and two children, the family first lived in a refugee camp in Iran. There, the patient started feeling ill about 6 months ago and was treated with tablets for several weeks and intragluteal injections. His symptoms subsided whilst on medication but recurred after the treatment ended. After crossing Turkey and Eastern Europe, the family reached Germany 4 months ago. All medical documents were lost during the journey.

The patient is afebrile and in fair general condition. Vital signs are normal. On examination, there is marked spinal tenderness in the lumbar region. The remaining examination is unremarkable.

Differential blood count, liver and renal function tests as well as LDH are normal. C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate are slightly raised at 26 mg/L (< 5 mg/L) and 40 mm/hour (< 20 mm/hour), respectively. Urinalysis is unremarkable.

MRI of the spine reveals signal enhancement of the L3 and L4 vertebral bodies, the corresponding vertebral disc and the right psoas muscle, as well as disc space narrowing and irregularities of both adjacent vertebral endplates (Fig. 81.1A and B). A chest X-ray shows no abnormalities.

What are the most likely differential diagnoses in this patient?

A 32-year-old Malawian woman presents with a 3-week history of headache and blurred vision. The headache has been gradual in onset and does not respond to over-the-counter painkillers. There is no fever and no history of convulsions or of head trauma. She received presumptive antimalarial treatment (artemether/lumefantrine) and a course of antibiotics (amoxicillin 500mg tds for 5 days), which was of no benefit. On examination, the patient appears wasted and slightly anaemic. All vital signs are normal and she is afebrile. The GCS is 15/15. There is no neck stiffness. The visual acuity is normal on both sides. On left lateral gaze there is an abduction deficit of the left eye with ‘blurring of vision’ reported by the patient (Fig. 35.1). The rest of the examination is normal. Laboratory results show a WBC count of 3.7 x10/L, hemoglobin of 10.2 g/dL, MCV of 92 fL, platelets of 91 x10°/L, and a fasting blood glucose of 5.43 mmol/L. Malaria RDT is negative (Table 35.1). A lumbar puncture was done on admission. The CSF looked clear, but the opening pressure was increased at 50 cmH2O (normal: 10-18 cmH2O). The CSF results are shown in Table 35.2: leukocytes 18 cells/μL, protein 0.8 g/L, glucose 1.97 mmol/L, India Ink negative, and culture positive for C. neoformans.

What are your differential diagnoses?

A 31-year-old woman is referred to a hospital in northern Tanzania with a loss of power and feeling in her legs. She describes being perfectly well up until 2 days earlier when she felt acute back pain which radiated band-like to the level of her umbilicus. The pain was severe, continuous, burning and unrelieved by analgesics or position. Within 12 hours the pain had lessened but she developed numbness in her feet and legs ascending to the level of her waist, loss of power in her legs and loss of control of her bladder. There is a history of a febrile illness 3 weeks previously, treated as malaria. There is no past or family history of similar illness and no history of trauma. She is married with 3 children, the last born is 12 months old. She does not smoke or take alcohol, and her HIV status during her last pregnancy was negative.

Clinically, she is well nourished with normal vital signs. General examination is unremarkable; there is no spinal tenderness, deformity or gibbus. On neurological examination she is fully orientated and higher mental functions appear normal. Cranial nerves including fundoscopy and upper limbs are normal. She is unable to move her legs and examination of the lower limbs reveals a flaccid paraparesis with a sensory level at T10 (Fig. 48.1). Tone is reduced bilaterally, power is reduced (MRC grade 1/5) in all muscle groups. Reflexes are absent bilaterally, and plantar reflexes are extensor. Sensation is reduced to light touch to the level of the umbilicus. Joint position sense is impaired in the feet and ankles, and vibration sense is absent to the anterior iliac crest bilaterally.

Her full blood count, renal and liver function tests were normal. Results of further blood tests are shown in Table 48.2. A spinal tap was done. The CSF opening pressure was normal and looked clear. Further CSF results are shown in Table 48.3. The X-rays of her chest and thoracolumbar spine were normal.

What is the clinical syndrome and where is the lesion?

A 35-year-old Caucasian male presents to a clinic in the United States with fatigue and a rash on his neck that started as a papule 2 days earlier. The lesion is non-pruritic, but it is associated with significant non-painful swelling and a pressure sensation in the neck. There is no history of fever, but the patient reports at least one episode of diaphoresis with mild confusion and headache. The patient recalls a break in the skin at the site of the lesion 3 days before while shaving and is sure that he has not been bitten by an insect. He has had no contact with animals and no foreign travel within the previous year. He had come to the clinic 24 hours earlier with similar symptoms. After blood cultures were obtained, he was given one dose of a first-generation cephalosporin and discharged on a ten-day oral course. He returns because of worsening malaise and neck swelling associated with mild difficulty breathing. The past medical history is unremarkable. The patient is a postal worker by profession.

Examination reveals a $2 \mathrm { c m }$ irregularly shaped, indurated non-tender patch on the left anterior neck with mild overlying erythema and several 2 to $3 \mathrm { m m }$ vesicles. The main lesion has a $6 \mathrm { m m }$ shallow ulceration. There is massive neck oedema making lymph nodes difficult to assess (see Fig. 21.1). His neck circumference had increased from $5 7 \mathrm { c m }$ at baseline to a peak of $8 1 \mathrm { c m }$ . Temperature is $3 6 . 9 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ $( 9 8 . 4 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { F } )$ , pulse $1 1 8 \mathrm { b p m }$ , blood pressure $1 3 8 / 9 0 \mathrm { m m H g }$ and respiratory rate 20 breath cycles per minute. The remainder of the initial physical examination is normal.

Full blood count, $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ , $\mathrm { C l } ^ { - } \mathrm { H C O } _ { 3 }$ , BUN, creatinine and random glucose are normal except for a mildly elevated haemoglobin at $1 8 . 7 \mathrm { g / d L }$ (reference range: $1 3 . 0 { - } 1 8 . 0 \mathrm { g } / \mathrm { d L } )$ .

What are the distinguishing features of this lesion that help narrow down your differential diagnosis?

A 32-year-old woman of African descent, born in Europe, presented with fever, abnormal behavior, and subsequent confusion 18 days after returning from a visit to rural Jos, Nigeria. On examination, she had a temperature of 37.5°C (99.5°F), mild jaundice, and a Glasgow Coma Scale of 14/15. She had no rash, palpable lymph nodes, or injected sclerae, but exhibited fine crepitations at the lung bases. Initial laboratory tests were refused due to concerns about recent rural exposure in an area known for viral hemorrhagic fever (Lassa). Laboratory results revealed a Plasmodium falciparum parasite count of 18% and a plasma creatinine of 430 μmol/L (reference range 45-90 μmol/L), indicating acute kidney injury. Urine output did not respond to fluid challenges, ruling out pre-renal failure. She was treated with intravenous artesunate, reducing the parasite count to 5%, but subsequently lapsed into a deep coma and developed renal failure requiring haemofiltration. After parasite clearance on day 5, her consciousness improved, but she developed laboured breathing and chest radiography findings suggestive of ARDS, necessitating prolonged respiratory support. What is the differential diagnosis?

A 3-year-old rural Lao boy presents to the ENT clinic with a 10-day history of gradual, painful swelling of the right cheek with associated fever and poor appetite. Three days previously his mother noticed a purulent discharge from the ear. He has no cough, vomiting or diarrhoea. There is no history of previous ear infection or dental problems and no known history of trauma. The child is developing normally and is up to date with vaccinations. His parents are rice farmers.

Clinical examination reveals the child looks unwell, with a fever of 39.5°C (103.1°F). There is a localized, fluctuant, hot, tender swelling below and anterior to the right ear, 6 to 8 cm in diameter, extending from the lower cheek to the submandibular region and consistent with a parotid mass (Fig. 15.1). Ear examination reveals a purulent discharge in the auditory canal and suspicion of a small fistula from which the pus is arising, with a right lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy. The oral cavity and throat are unremarkable. There is no lymphadenopathy and no hepatosplenomegaly. Heart sounds are normal and the chest is clear.

Laboratory results show WBC 16.5 x 10^9/L (4-10 x 10^9/L), 90% neutrophils. Hb 9.4 g/dL (13-15 g/dL), all other blood tests are normal.

What are your differential diagnoses?

A 72-year-old male farmer is admitted to a provincial hospital in northern Laos with extensive, painful verrucous skin lesions on his left foot and lower leg. Ten years prior, he had a leech bite on the dorsum of his left foot. One week later a small painless red nodule developed at the site of the bite. Over the following years the lesion slowly increased in size; further lesions developed and spread up to his knee. Three days before admission his ankle became painful and swollen. Vital signs are normal and the patient is afebrile. His left lower leg and foot are grossly swollen (Fig. 25.1); the skin is hyperaemic and feels hot. There are several cauliflower-like masses and oval plaque-like lesions on his left lower leg and foot. The lesions are partly erythematous, partly fungating and purulent, oozing a bad odour. Radiography of the left leg and foot showed no bone involvement. What are the important differential diagnoses?

A 4-year-old girl from rural eastern Uganda is brought to the Accident and Emergency Department in a coma. Her father reports she was well until yesterday when she developed a headache followed by shaking chills. The family suspected malaria and planned to seek care in the morning, but she developed a 10-minute seizure at 5 a.m. and has remained unconscious for the past 4 hours. There is no history of head trauma. Her temperature is 38.7°C (101.7°F), pulse is 150 bpm, respiratory rate is 36 breaths per minute, and blood pressure is 98/40 mmHg. Physical examination reveals no neck stiffness or jaundice, normal capillary refill, nasal flaring, and a Blantyre Coma Scale of 1/5. Pupils are 2 mm and reactive, extraocular movements are normal, and there is no papilloedema. Decerebrate posturing is observed with stimulation. Cardiac examination reveals a gallop rhythm, and the liver is palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin, with the spleen palpable 4 cm below the left costal margin. A rapid glucose test is normal. Laboratory results show a haematocrit of 17.6% (reference ≥30%), a platelet count of 28 x10^9/L (reference 150-450), and a positive malaria rapid diagnostic test (RDT) (Table 4.1). What is the differential diagnosis?

A 16-year-old Sri Lankan boy presents to a local hospital with fever, frontal headache and severe body aches for 2 days. He has vomited two to three times during the illness and has not passed any urine for the previous 12 hours. He does not have a cough, coryza or shortness of breath. He has been attending school until his illness. He had been fishing in an urban water stream 5 days before falling ill. On examination, the boy appears ill and drowsy. He is jaundiced and has subconjunctival haemorrhages (Fig. 27.1). Temperature is $3 8 . 3 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ $( 1 0 0 . 9 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { F } )$ , the pulse rate is $1 0 0 \mathrm { b p m }$ (low in volume). The blood pressure is $9 0 / 6 0 \mathrm { m m H g }$ . There is no neck stiffness, however there is severe muscle tenderness, mainly involving the abdominal wall and the calves such that the patient finds it difficult to walk. There is no lymphadenopathy. The cardiac apex is not shifted and heart sounds are clear. Examination of the lungs is normal. The liver is palpable at $4 \mathrm { c m }$ below the right costal margin and is tender. The spleen is not palpable. There is mild bilateral renal angle tenderness. Neurological examination is normal. Laboratory results are as follows: WBC 5.7 (68%: 31%), Haemoglobin 14.8 g/dL, Platelets 96 ×10^9/L, AST 64 IU/L, ALT 58 IU/L, ALP 246 IU/L, Serum bilirubin total 77 umol/L, Serum bilirubin direct 54.7 μmol/L, Blood urea nitrogen 20.7 μmol/L, Serum creatinine 212.2 umol/L, C-reactive protein 48 mg/L (Table 27.1). Urine microscopy shows 20 red blood cells per high-power field, proteins $\mathbf { \omega } ^ { \mathrm { { c } } } + \mathbf { \omega } ^ { \mathrm { { c } } }$ and granular casts $\mathbf { \omega } ^ { \mathrm { { c } } } + \mathbf { \omega } ^ { \mathrm { { c } } }$ . A chest radiograph is normal. An ECG shows sinus tachycardia.

What is the most likely diagnosis and what are your differentials?

A 7-year-old girl from Lima, Peru, presents with a chronic skin lesion on her nose that appeared 4 months ago as a small nodule and slowly turned into an ulcer. The lesion is slightly itchy but not painful, and there is no history of trauma. The girl is otherwise healthy and travelled to a valley on the western slopes of the Andes 6 months ago. On examination, the lesion is a localized ulcer approximately 2 cm in diameter with indurated borders and plaque-like infiltration of the surrounding skin. There are no palpable lymph nodes, and the rest of the physical examination is normal. She is afebrile. A photograph of the lesion is shown (Fig. 2.1).

What are your differential diagnoses?

A 16-year-old Malawian girl presents to the emergency room with fever, generalized abdominal pain, and frontal headache for the past 5 days. She delivered a baby 5 months ago, and an HIV test done during antenatal care was negative. Her past medical history is unremarkable. She lives in an urban high-density area with limited access to running water and electricity.

On examination, she is in fair nutritional state with a temperature of 38.1°C (100.6°F), blood pressure of 110/60 mmHg, pulse of 78 bpm, respiratory rate of 20 breaths per minute, and a Glasgow Coma Scale of 15/15. She exhibits mild scleral jaundice and diffuse abdominal tenderness without guarding. The liver is not enlarged, but the spleen is palpable 2 cm below the left costal margin. The chest is clear, and there is no lymphadenopathy. Pelvic examination is unremarkable.

Laboratory results on admission are as follows (Table 13.1): WBC 3.2 x10^9/L (reference 4-10), Hemoglobin 10.9 mg/dL (reference 12-14), MCV 90 fL (reference 80-99), Platelets 164 x 10^9/L (reference 150-400), Creatinine 71 umol/L (reference <80). A blood film for malaria parasites is positive, with “low” parasitemia. Liver function tests are not available due to reagent stock issues.

What are your most important differential diagnoses? How would you approach this patient?

A 52-year-old man is brought to an urban hospital in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam because of abdominal pain and vomiting. He describes 4 days of retro-orbital headache, lethargy, myalgia and fevers that had begun to improve over the last 24 hours. He has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and poorly controlled hypertension. His last travel outside the city was several years ago. On examination, the patient is drowsy, but rousable, with a Glasgow Coma Score (GCS) of 14/15, temperature 36.5°C, blood pressure 105/90 mmHg, heart rate 120 bpm, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and peripheral oxygen saturation 93% on air. He has a weak radial pulse, but normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination reveals a dull percussion note and reduced breath sounds at both lung bases. He has mild abdominal distension, with shifting dullness and a tender 3 cm liver edge. Skin examination is unremarkable. Laboratory results show: Haemoglobin 14.6 g/dL, Haematocrit 53.9%, Platelets 58 x 10°/L, WCC 2.1 x10°/L, Neutrophils 0.9 x 10°/L, Lymphocytes 0.8 x10°/L, C-reactive protein 20 mg/L, Urea 7.8 mmol/L, Creatinine 114 umol/L, Alanine aminotransferase 812 U/L, Alkaline phosphatase 260 U/L, Total bilirubin 18 umol/L, Lactate 3.5 mmol/L (Table 1). What are the main differential diagnoses to consider?

A 27-year-old male Swiss tourist presented with a 3.5-week history of travel in the rainforests of the Amazon Basin in northern Peru. During the second week of his stay, he developed an acute febrile illness with chills, malaise, frontal headache, generalized myalgia, and a transient, non-pruritic maculopapular rash that started on the forearms and spread to the trunk, neck, and face before fading after 3 days. He also experienced slowly progressive debilitating polyarthralgias affecting the peripheral joints, accompanied by transient joint swelling. Painful cervical and inguinal lymphadenopathy was also noted, which resolved after about 1 week. He was initially diagnosed with dengue fever at a local hospital and received symptomatic treatment with paracetamol. While the fever and other symptoms subsided within 1 week, the polyarthralgias did not improve and showed a symmetrical pattern mainly affecting the small joints of the hands and feet, as well as the wrists, ankles, and knees. Upon returning to Switzerland, his general practitioner performed laboratory tests, including serological testing for dengue virus, chikungunya virus, parvovirus B19, Epstein-Barr virus, Borrelia burgdorferi, Chlamydia trachomatis, Salmonella Typhi, and S. Paratyphi, all of which were negative. After two months of persistent joint pain, he was referred to a rheumatologist and subsequently to a tropical medicine clinic. Physical examination was unremarkable, with no clinical signs of inflammation in the affected joints. Full blood count was normal, and C-reactive protein was mildly elevated at 9 mg/L (<5). Liver function tests were normal. (Fig 87.1, Fig 87.2)

What are your differential diagnoses?

A 24-year-old Dutch yoga instructor presents to an emergency room in Berlin, Germany, with one episode of strange sensations in the right side of her body. This started in the right side of her face, marched to her right arm and then continued to involve her right leg. She describes the feeling as ‘pins and needles’ lasting for about 2 minutes. She had a similar episode several months ago. Four years before this presentation, after finishing school, she had left her home town in The Netherlands to go backpacking for 2 years. She travelled extensively through South America (Ecuador, Peru, Argentina) and South-east Asia (Thailand, Laos, Cambodia), staying in hostels or private accommodations. She describes herself as an ‘eco-traveller’, visiting the countryside and staying with local people. She has been a strict vegan for the past 8 years. She would eat food from local vendors but never any animal products. Her main diet during her travelling consisted of fruits, vegetables, nuts and rice.

On examination she looks well and is afebrile. Her neurological examination is completely unremarkable. The rest of her physical examination is also normal. Her routine blood investigations, including differential blood count and C-reactive protein are completely normal. Her CSF examination is unremarkable. The MRI of her brain with gadolinium enhancement shows multiple cortical and subcortical cystic lesions in both hemispheres (Fig. 38.1).

What is the clinical syndrome the patient presents with and what is the most likely diagnosis in light of the imaging findings and the patient’s travel history?

A 21-year-old male migrant from rural Mali is referred to the tropical medicine department of a university hospital in Germany. He was previously evaluated for splenomegaly and bicytopenia at the haematology department, but a diagnosis could not be established. The patient reports intermittent fever and a feeling of “heaviness” on the left side of his abdomen for an unspecified duration. He denies night sweats and reports stable weight. He migrated from rural Mali to Germany 1 year prior, traveling through Niger, Libya, and Italy. He is unable to read and write. Clinically, the patient appears well. His temperature is 36.1°C (96.98°F), BP is 120/80 mmHg, and pulse is 64 bpm. The spleen is massively enlarged (around 15 cm below the left costal margin), but there is no clinical anaemia or lymphadenopathy. Heart sounds are clear, and the rest of the examination is normal. Abdominal ultrasound reveals a spleen measuring 21.8 cm in longitudinal diameter with homogenous parenchyma. The liver is normal in size and appearance, and the flow of the portal and splenic veins is normal. There is no lymphadenopathy or free fluid. Laboratory results are as follows: WBC 3.3 x 10^9/L, neutrophils 2.29 x 10^9/L, lymphocytes 1.4 x 10^9/L, monocytes 0.28 x 10^9/L, eosinophils 0.12 x 10^9/L, haemoglobin 13.8 g/dL, platelets 124 x 10^9/L, LDH 185 U/L, total bilirubin 0.5 mg/dL, IgM 8.59 g/l, CRP 0.5, ESR 9/21 mm/h, Plasmodium spp. (thick and thin film) negative, P. falciparum IFAT 1:256 (Table 73.1).

What are the most important differential diagnoses in this patient?

A 31-year-old Guatemalan man with no past medical history presents with several minutes of weakness and numbness of the leg, which resolved before arrival at the hospital. He also had two episodes of facial twitching two weeks prior, each lasting 10 seconds. He was born and lived in a rural area of Guatemala, where his family owned uncorralled pigs and his house lacked sanitation services. He immigrated to New York 5 years ago. His vitals were normal. Cranial nerves were intact. Motor and sensory examinations were normal. Deep tendon reflexes and gait were normal. Cell blood count and serum chemistry were within normal limits. A computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) on admission are shown in Fig. 82.1 and Fig. 82.2. A CT angiography showed patent cerebral arteries.

A 12-year-old boy is brought to a health centre in rural north-west Kenya with a 2-month history of painful, watery, red eyes, worsened by sunlight. He was previously treated with tetracycline eye ointment without improvement and subsequently received juice extracts from the ecucuka plant (Aloe vera species), which caused severe pain and discharge. He lives in a hot, dusty area and helps with herding. On examination, his visual acuity is 6/60 in the left eye and hand movements in the right eye. The right eye shows fibrotic lids with loss of lid architecture and tightening of palpebral aperture, loss of lower lid lashes, and in-turned upper lid lashes (trichiasis). The conjunctiva is severely inflamed with >5 follicles. The cornea shows diffuse opacification with central thinning and fibrovascular pannus. The left eye has swollen lids, mucus deposits, misdirected eyelashes, and eversion of the lower lid margin. The cornea shows focal inferocentral scars, one with adherent iris indicating previous perforation, and a thin central cornea. The anterior chamber is shallow in the left eye and not visible in the right eye. The pupil is distorted towards the leucoma in the left eye and not visible in the right eye (Fig. 30.1 and Fig. 30.2). Findings on inspection of both eyes are summarized in Table 30.1.

What are your differential diagnoses?

A 55-year-old woman presents to a hospital in rural Vietnam with a 1-day history of fever, headache and vomiting. Her blood film is negative for malaria and she is treated with fluids and paracetamol. On the second day of illness she develops confusion and is referred to a hospital in Ho Chi Minh City for further investigation. The patient has a history of type 2 diabetes and hypertension, she has been on treatment for 4 years. She raises pigs on her smallholding and works as a butcher in a local market selling pork and chicken. On admission, she is confused with a Glasgow Coma Score of 12/15 (E3 M5 V4), there is fever (38.5 °C or 101.3 °F), tachycardia (124 bpm), hypotension (85/60 mmHg), tachypnoea (32 breaths per minute), and hypoxia (O2 saturation 86% on ambient air). She has neck stiffness and photophobia. There are no focal neurological signs. She has a diffuse petechial rash over her trunk (Fig. 85.1) and marked purpuric non-blanching lesions on her left leg (Fig. 85.2). The rest of her examination is unremarkable. Her laboratory results on admission are shown in Table 85.1. Non-contrast-enhanced CT scan of the brain is unremarkable. Electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia and is otherwise normal.
